en: Majjhima Nikāya 141,
Saccavibhaṅgasutta:
Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus!"
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, by the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana...”
The unsurpassed Wheel of Dhamma has been set in motion, which cannot be turned back by any ascetic or brahmin,
by any deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world—
that is to say, the proclaiming, teaching, making known, establishing, revealing, analyzing, and clarifying of the Four Noble Truths.
Of which four?
The announcing, teaching, making known, establishing, revealing, analyzing, and clarifying of the noble truth of suffering;
the announcing, teaching, making known, and establishing of the noble truth of the origin of suffering.

The explaining, the detailing, the making plain; the announcing, the teaching, the proclaiming, the establishing, the revealing, the analyzing, the making plain of the noble truth of the cessation of suffering;
the announcing, the teaching, the proclaiming, the establishing, the revealing, the analyzing, the making plain of the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
“Monks, by the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the unsurpassed Wheel of Dhamma has been set in motion at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana—
a wheel that cannot be turned back by any ascetic or brahmin, by any deva, Māra, or Brahmā,
or by anyone in the world; that is to say:”
This is the announcing, the teaching, the making known, the establishing, the revealing, the analyzing, and the elucidating of these Four Noble Truths.
Bhikkhus, serve Sāriputta and Moggallāna;
associate with Sāriputta and Moggallāna.
The wise bhikkhus are supporters of their fellow celibates.
Just as, bhikkhus, is a father, so is Sāriputta;
just as one who nurtures what has been born, so is Moggallāna.
“Bhikkhus, Sāriputta guides others toward the fruit of stream-entry; Moggallāna [guides them] toward the supreme goal.
Bhikkhus, Sāriputta is capable of explaining, teaching, proclaiming, establishing, disclosing, analyzing, and elucidating the Four Noble Truths in detail.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Having said this, the Sugata rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.
There, not long after the Blessed One had departed, the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus:
"Friends, bhikkhus!"
“Friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Sāriputta.
The Venerable Sāriputta said this:
“Friends, by the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana, the unsurpassed—”
The Wheel of Dhamma has been set in motion by the ascetic, or by a brahmin, or by a deva, or by Māra, or by Brahmā,
or by anyone in the world, such that it cannot be stopped;
that is to say, the announcing, teaching, making known, establishing, revealing, analyzing, and clarifying of the Four Noble Truths.
Of which four?
The proclamation, teaching, making known, establishing, revealing, analyzing, and clarifying of the noble truth of suffering;
the proclamation, teaching, making known, establishing... of the noble truth of the origin of suffering.
The exposition, analysis, and clarification; the announcing, teaching, proclaiming, establishing, expounding, analyzing, and clarifying of the noble truth of the cessation of suffering;
the announcing, teaching, proclaiming, establishing, expounding, analyzing, and clarifying of the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
And what, friends, is the noble truth of suffering?

Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, death is suffering; sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are suffering; not to obtain what one desires is suffering; in short, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering.
And what, friends, is birth?
Whatever birth, taking birth, descent, coming-to-be, manifestation of the aggregates, and acquisition of the sense-bases there is for those various beings in their respective classes of beings—
this, friends, is called ‘birth.
And what, friends, is aging?

Whatever aging, decrepitude, brokenness, graying, wrinkling, and decline of the life-force occurs among various beings in their respective classes of beings, and whatever ripening of the faculties there is—
this, friends, is called ‘aging.
And what, friends, is death?

The passing away, the decease, the breaking up, the disappearance, the death, the dying, the completion of time, the dissolution of the aggregates, the laying down of the body, the cutting off of the life-faculty of this or that being from this or that class of beings—
this, friends, is called “death. And what, friends, is sorrow?

"Friends, when one who is beset by some kind of misfortune or touched by some kind of painful state experiences sorrow, lamentation, and a state of being sorrowful— an inner sorrow, an inner anguish— this, friends,
is called 'sorrow.
And what, friends, is lamentation?"

"Friends, when one who is beset by some kind of misfortune or touched by some kind of painful state cries out, laments, wails, and bewails— this crying out, lamenting, wailing, and bewailing, this state of crying out and lamenting,
friends, is called 'lamentation' (parideva).
And what, friends, is suffering (dukkha)?"
"Whatever, friends, is bodily pain, bodily discomfort, painful and unpleasant feeling born of body-contact—
this, friends, is called 'suffering.
And what, friends, is mental grief?"
That which, friends, is mental pain, mental displeasure, painful and unpleasant feeling born of mind-contact—
this, friends, is called ‘grief.
And what, friends, is despair?

"Friends, for one who is possessed of some particular misfortune or touched by some particular state of suffering, the distress, the despair, the state of being distressed, and the state of being despaired—
this, friends, is called 'despair. And what, friends,
is that which is not obtaining what one desires, which is also suffering?"
Friends, for beings subject to birth, such a wish arises:
"O, that we were not subject to birth! O, that birth would not come upon us!
Yet this cannot be attained by mere wishing.
This too is: "Not to get what one wishes for is suffering.
For beings subject to aging, friends...
for beings subject to illness, friends...
Friends, for beings subject to death...
for beings subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, such a wish arises:
"O, that we were not subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair! O, that sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would not come upon us!"
But this is not to be obtained by mere wishing.
This too is: “Not to get what one wishes for is suffering.
And what, friends, in brief, are the five aggregates of clinging that are suffering?

That is to say: the form aggregate subject to clinging, the feeling aggregate subject to clinging, the perception aggregate subject to clinging, the volitional formations aggregate subject to clinging, and the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging.
These, friends, are called "in brief, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering.
This, friends, is called "the noble truth of suffering."
And what, friends, is the noble truth of the origin of suffering?
It is this craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there;
namely, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence.
This, friends, is called the noble truth of the origin of suffering.
And what, friends, is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering?
It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving—its relinquishing, its renouncing, its liberation, and the absence of attachment to it.
This, friends, is called ‘the noble truth of the cessation of suffering.
And what, friends, is the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering?
It is this very noble eightfold path; that is to say: [the right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration].”
Right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
And what, friends, is right view?
It is, friends, the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of the origin of suffering, the knowledge of the cessation of suffering, and the knowledge of the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
This, friends, is called right view.
And what, friends, is right intention?
The intention of renunciation, the intention of non-ill will, and the intention of non-cruelty.
This, friends, is called right intention.
And what, friends, is right speech?
Abstinence from false speech, abstinence from malicious speech, abstinence from harsh speech, and abstinence from idle chatter.
This, friends, is called right speech.
And what, friends, is right action?
It is abstaining from taking life, abstaining from taking what is not given, and abstaining from sexual misconduct.
This, friends, is called right action.
And what, friends, is right livelihood?
Here, friends, a noble disciple, having abandoned wrong livelihood, makes his living by means of right livelihood.
This, friends, is called right livelihood. And what, friends, is right effort?

Here, friends, a bhikkhu generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts the mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states; he generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts the mind, and strives for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states; he generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts the mind, and strives for the arising of unarisen wholesome states; he generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts the mind, and strives for the maintenance, non-confusion, increase, expansion, and fulfillment by development of arisen wholesome states. This, friends, is called right effort.
He generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the abandoning of evil, unwholesome states that have arisen;
he generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the arising of wholesome states that have not yet arisen;

he generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the stability, non-confusion, increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of wholesome states that have arisen.
This, friends, is called right effort.
And what, friends, is right mindfulness?
Here, friends, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body as the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings …pe… he dwells contemplating the mind in the mind … he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena,
ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
This, friends, is called “right mindfulness.
And what, friends, is right concentration?

Here, friends, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion.

With the stilling of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without applied and sustained thought, and possesses the rapture and happiness born of concentration.
And with the fading away of rapture, he dwells equanimous … [as before] … he enters and dwells in the third jhāna … [as before] … he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.
This, friends, is called ‘right concentration.
This, friends, is called ‘the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
At Bārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Isipatana, this unsurpassed [Dhamma wheel] was set in motion by the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
"The Wheel of Dhamma has been set in motion by the ascetic, or by a brahmin, or by a deva, or by Māra, or by Brahmā,
or by anyone in the world, which is irreversible—
that is to say, the announcing, teaching, proclaiming, establishing, revealing, analyzing, and elucidating of these Four Noble Truths."
This is what the Venerable Sāriputta said.
The monks were satisfied and rejoiced in the words of the Venerable Sāriputta.
The Eleventh Discourse, the Analysis of Truths (Saccavibhaṅgasutta), is finished.
